summary: Steve Eisman interviews Evercore Fed watcher Krishna Guha on Fed chair Warsh's hike, his limits on QE and forward guidance, and Bessent's Treasury buybacks. Guha attributes the 10y rise to ~5.25% to AI-hyperscaler and deficit borrowing, a higher AI-era neutral rate, oil/diesel and Fed opacity; buybacks too small and credibility-damaging. 5%+ yields strain non-AI economy and housing; watch whether stocks hold up given wealth-effect-driven consumption.

coverage.note: Warsh hike rationale (expectations de-anchoring); Guha view: tariff and oil inflation transitory; insurance hike
Warsh supply-side framework; QE debate (Eisman asset prices vs Guha ZLB/long rates/wealth channel); balance sheet size
QE cost-of-capital channel; Warsh QE only in emergencies; QT announcement risk and conditional QT restart; 10y 4.5% -> 5.25%
Drivers of yield rise: hyperscaler + deficit borrowing, AI-driven higher r*, oil/diesel, hike-path uncertainty; forward guidance definition (not a claim)
Fed communication makes policy effective; 30-year move to guidance; Greenspan anecdote and sponsor read skipped
Greenspan easing/tightening bias; strong-form guidance risk; Warsh removal of guard rails -> rates overshoot
Bessent buybacks as operation twist; off-the-run liquidity; size too small; two-sided risk for leveraged shorts
LCR reform reserves -> Treasuries; issuance-mix signaling; intervention credibility cost; AI less rate sensitive
Two-halves economy: 5% hurts non-AI/housing; 6% for AI capex; AI stocks under pressure; import leakage and wealth effects; Greenspan rating (no claim)
Greenspan regulation -> GFC; Bernanke crisis toolkit; Yellen low-for-longer recovery
Powell 2020 private credit backstop; slow then fast tightening; soft landing vs recession consensus; tariffs -> import price inflation
Markets trade with oil and 10y; rest is wrap-up repeating earlier points and disclaimer

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you've just been above target for so long you worry that people are going to start to just expect higher inflation and then factor that in to their wage negotiations
claims.claim: After years of inflation above target the Fed can no longer look through supply shocks (tariffs, oil) because persistent overshoots risk de-anchoring expectations into wage and price setting, which justified Warsh's hike.
claims.conditions: when inflation has exceeded target for a long time, even if shocks are supply-driven
claims.testable: partly - duration of above-target inflation vs Fed hikes can be coded; expectations channel harder

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: I do think that the tariff inflation is going to drop into, you know, drop out of the numbers fairly soon.
claims.claim: Tariff-driven inflation is a one-off price-level effect that will drop out of year-on-year inflation numbers soon, so inflation should gradually fall.
claims.conditions: if no further tariff rounds
claims.testable: yes - track tariff-exposed goods inflation after tariff dates

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: I don't see any evidence that oil is going to create some kind of lasting inflation impulse.
claims.claim: The current oil price shock is not expected to create a lasting inflation impulse (no second-round effects seen yet).
claims.direction: core inflation not lifted persistently by oil
claims.conditions: absent second-round effects in wages/expectations
claims.testable: yes - oil shocks vs subsequent core inflation persistence

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the labor market, the jobs market is in pretty good shape is telling you that maybe it's a good time to take out some insurance on the inflation side
claims.claim: A strong labor market gives the Fed room to take out 'insurance' hikes against inflation, though Guha sees this insurance as dispensable with inflation cooling.
claims.indicator: labor market strength, recent inflation prints
claims.conditions: strong jobs market; less compelling when inflation is already cooling
claims.testable: partly - Fed reaction to labor slack can be modeled

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: he thinks that developments in the economy are driven less by what happens on the demand side of the economy, the spending side if you like, right? And more by what's happening on the supply side.
claims.claim: Warsh replaces the New Keynesian demand-management framework with a supply-side view (productivity, labor-force incentives), changing the models and guideposts the Fed uses to set rates.
claims.conditions: under Warsh's chairmanship
claims.testable: no - framework shift, hard to test directly

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: my personal opinion is that quantitative easing did absolutely nothing to help the actual economy, but inflated asset prices.
claims.claim: Eisman's view: QE inflated asset prices without helping the real economy.
claims.direction: asset prices up, real economy unaffected
claims.testable: partly - asset-price vs real-activity response to QE episodes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the only thing you can do is to start working on pulling down longer term interest rates. And the way you do that is by buying assets.
claims.claim: At the zero lower bound QE lowers long-term rates by buying assets, which works partly by raising asset values and wealth that then support consumer spending.
claims.direction: long yields down, asset prices up, consumption up
claims.conditions: when policy rate is at zero and demand is very weak (GFC, pandemic)
claims.testable: yes - yield and asset moves around QE announcements

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Down from about 9 trillion at the peak.
claims.claim: The Fed balance sheet is about $6.5-7 trillion, down from about $9 trillion at the peak, after QE grew it from roughly nothing pre-2008.
claims.testable: yes - H.4.1 data

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: a company's borrowing rate will be the government's borrowing rate plus some kind of spread. So if the Fed buys the government bonds, pushes down the price of government borrowing
claims.claim: QE lowers the corporate cost of capital because corporate borrowing costs equal government yields plus a spread, so lower Treasury yields boost investment and hiring.
claims.direction: corporate borrowing costs down, investment up
claims.testable: yes - corporate yield pass-through from Treasury moves

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: that kind of uh QE that goes on and on and on is achieving relatively little at large cost in terms of bloating out the central bank's balance sheet and asset prices
claims.claim: Warsh sees a role for QE when markets seize up, but QE continued into recoveries achieves little at large cost (bloated balance sheet, inflated asset prices), so he will confine it to emergencies.
claims.indicator: market functioning stress; Fed balance sheet
claims.conditions: QE useful only when markets seize up (GFC, early pandemic)
claims.testable: partly - compare QE effects in crisis vs recovery episodes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: if he just announces tomorrow that he's going to dump a whole load of Treasury bonds and mortgage bonds into the market, he will drive long-term interest rates to the sky.
claims.claim: Announcing large, fast Fed sales of Treasuries and MBS would push long-term rates sharply higher, so balance-sheet reduction must be gradual.
claims.direction: long yields up on QT announcements
claims.conditions: especially when long yields are already high
claims.testable: yes - yield reaction to QT announcements (2013 taper, 2017, 2022)

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: I think he's going to look for a window of opportunity when bond market conditions stabilize, when yields come down some
claims.claim: Warsh will restart balance-sheet shrinkage only once bond markets stabilize and yields fall, so QT is conditional on lower yields.
claims.conditions: bond market stable, yields lower
claims.testable: partly - observable once plans are announced

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the 10 year has gone from something like 4 and a.5% to today I think it was 5 point a little bit over 5.2 two at one point.
claims.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield rose from about 4.5% in July to about 5.25% at recording (early October 2026).
claims.testable: yes - yield data

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: there are more borrowers competing for savings competing for capital and so that's bidding up the the the rate they have to pay.
claims.claim: Heavy AI-hyperscaler debt issuance on top of a 6%-of-GDP federal deficit means more borrowers compete for savings, which bids up yields (private sector crowding out government).
claims.indicator: hyperscaler bond issuance; federal deficit % of GDP (6%)
claims.conditions: large deficits plus private capex borrowing
claims.testable: yes - corporate + Treasury net issuance vs term premium

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: we've moved from a world where there was too much saving chasing too few investment opportunities to a world in which there's a huge demand to invest chasing a limited pool of savings
claims.claim: A multi-year AI investment boom shifts the economy from a savings glut to strong investment demand, raising the neutral rate (r*) so normal Fed funds and bond yields will be higher.
claims.conditions: while the AI investment boom lasts
claims.testable: partly - r* estimates (Laubach-Williams) vs capex cycles

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: But the our net upward pressure in oil again since the ceasefire broke down in the early summer with diesel prices at all-time highs, 100%. Is putting upward pressure on inflation and on bond yields.
claims.claim: Higher oil since the US-Iran ceasefire broke down, with diesel at all-time highs, is pushing up inflation and bond yields.
claims.conditions: during the Middle East conflict
claims.testable: yes - oil/diesel vs breakevens and yields

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you're not getting the full picture because refined product like diesel and jet fuel has actually increased a lot more than you would think
claims.claim: Crude (WTI/Brent) and gasoline understate the energy shock because refined products like diesel and jet fuel have risen far more (diesel roughly doubled, like oil near $200).
claims.indicator: diesel and jet fuel prices vs WTI/Brent (crack spreads)
claims.direction: refined products up more than crude
claims.conditions: supply disruption to refined products
claims.testable: yes - diesel/jet vs crude price data

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: there is also an aspect of this that has to do with bond investors looking at the Fed and saying, you know, how far are they planning to go with these rate hikes?
claims.claim: Uncertainty over how far the Fed will hike, because Warsh gives little explanation, adds to the rise in bond yields.
claims.conditions: when Fed gives little guidance during a hiking cycle
claims.testable: partly - yield vol around FOMC under low guidance

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: That markets work better, but policy also works better when the markets in particular and also the public understand what the central bank's trying to do, right?
claims.claim: Transparent central bank communication of its reaction function makes policy more effective and markets work better, since firms and markets can anticipate responses to shocks.
claims.testable: partly - market volatility/surprise around policy under different communication regimes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: So the Fed over the last 30 years or so, if we go back from the early Greenspan era, has steadily moved in the direction of doing more of both, right?
claims.claim: Over about 30 years since early Greenspan the Fed steadily moved to more forward guidance and strategy communication, so communication regimes differ across eras.
claims.testable: partly - regime dating for split-sample tests

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: It was Greenspan who introduced what was called an easing bias or a tightening bias in the Fed statement.
claims.claim: The Fed statement's easing/tightening bias (first forward guidance, late Greenspan) signaled whether the next move was more likely a hike or a cut.
claims.direction: next policy move in bias direction
claims.testable: yes - statement bias vs subsequent rate changes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: a central bank shouldn't project or communicate more confidence about the future than it than than than it really has
claims.claim: Strong-form calendar forward guidance is risky because it projects false certainty and can lock the central bank into wrong actions, so it should be an emergency tool only.
claims.conditions: acceptable in emergencies (pandemic, GFC), not normal times
claims.testable: partly - policy errors after explicit commitments

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Worshes removed those guard rails and that has contributed in my view to rates markets
claims.claim: By dropping broad reaction-function guidance Warsh has removed the guard rails around rates repricing, so markets that overshoot and must guess the Fed's criteria have run rampant.
claims.conditions: when Fed withholds reaction-function guidance amid big fundamental shocks
claims.testable: partly - rate vol under low-guidance vs high-guidance regimes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: issue short-term take that money, buy long.
claims.claim: Treasury buybacks financed with bills (an operation twist) aim to lower long-term yields by retiring long bonds and issuing short paper.
claims.direction: long yields down, bill supply up
claims.conditions: only if sized large relative to the market
claims.testable: yes - yields around buyback operations

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you have some kind of you know old bond issues that nobody really wants to buy because they're not traded much and so they tend to have a a a you know a lower price a higher yield
claims.claim: Old, illiquid off-the-run Treasuries trade at higher yields, so buying them back and issuing liquid on-the-run bonds is efficient for the Treasury but has little market-wide impact.
claims.indicator: off-the-run vs on-the-run Treasury yield spread
claims.testable: yes - on/off-the-run spreads

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: this is a 40 trillion market and you're coming up with you know a few billion here a few billion there right why bother
claims.claim: Buybacks of $4-6 billion per operation are far too small against a $40 trillion Treasury market to stabilize long yields.
claims.indicator: buyback size vs Treasury market size
claims.conditions: fails when intervention is tiny relative to market
claims.testable: yes - size vs yield impact

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you wanted to try to create some two-sided risk in the mind of particularly leveraged uh investors.
claims.claim: Small buyback operations may aim to create two-sided risk for leveraged investors (hedge funds) running one-way Treasury shorts and so damp overshooting.
claims.conditions: when positioning is one-way short
claims.testable: partly - positioning vs buyback days

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: reforming regulations in a way that in effect um encourages banks to hold fewer Fed reserves, which would help Kevin Walsh in his goal of bringing down the Fed balance sheet
claims.claim: Liquidity-rule reform (e.g., LCR) that tilts banks from Fed reserves to Treasuries would help shrink the Fed balance sheet and add Treasury demand, though banks may prefer bills over long bonds.
claims.indicator: LCR / bank liquidity rules; bank Treasury holdings
claims.conditions: demand concentrated at short tenors
claims.testable: partly - bank holdings after rule changes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: he's also sending a signal that future government debt issuance may be shifted from these longerterm bonds to the shorter duration bonds.
claims.claim: Buybacks signal that future Treasury issuance will shift toward shorter maturities, which can lower long yields today through expected supply.
claims.direction: long yields down on shorter issuance signals
claims.testable: yes - yields around refunding announcements

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: serious governments like the US government tend not to intervene in their own debt market. That's the sort of thing you find more often in struggling emerging markets
claims.claim: A government intervening in its own bond market signals difficulty selling debt and hurts credibility, which can raise rather than lower yields; Bessent's buybacks did not damp yields (10y about 5.25%).
claims.conditions: when intervention is small and looks like distress
claims.testable: partly - EM-style intervention episodes vs yields

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: The AI story is plausibly a lot less interest rate sensitive than other types of normal business activity.
claims.claim: AI investment is much less interest-rate sensitive than ordinary business activity because expected returns are huge, so the aggregate economy tolerates higher yields than before.
claims.conditions: until a breaking point in rates
claims.testable: partly - capex sensitivity to rates by sector

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: I think we're already clearly in territory you know with a five handle which is putting strain on the nonAI uh parts of the economy.
claims.claim: With 10-year yields above 5%, the non-AI economy is under strain and crowded out, with housing hit hardest as 7% mortgage rates leave it bombed out.
claims.conditions: 10y yield at or above 5%
claims.testable: yes - housing activity vs mortgage rates

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: that might require rates to go long-term borrowing costs to go even significantly higher from here say six handle or something
claims.claim: AI investment itself would likely be impaired only if long-term borrowing costs rise to about 6%.
claims.conditions: long rates around 6%+
claims.testable: partly - threshold not yet observed

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: we might be entering into territory where the AI stock price gains start to come under pressure
claims.claim: At current 10-year yields around 5%+, AI stock price gains may start to come under pressure.
claims.direction: AI stocks down as yields rise
claims.conditions: 10y around 5%+
claims.testable: yes - AI equity returns vs yield changes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: The AI investment spend a lot of it actually goes on imports.
claims.claim: AI capex leaks largely to imported chips while wealth-effect consumption is spent at home, so US demand depends heavily on wealth gains of high-end consumers.
claims.indicator: import content of AI capex; consumption by top income/wealth groups
claims.conditions: while wage gains lag costs for most consumers
claims.testable: partly - import share of capex, consumption by wealth quintile

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the one thing to watch right now is whether the stock market can withstand, you know, 10-year yields in this zip code because if the stock market sells off, then you have a wealth problem.
claims.claim: The key signal is whether stocks withstand ~5% 10-year yields; an equity sell-off would hit consumer wealth and spending.
claims.conditions: economy reliant on wealth effects at the top
claims.testable: yes - equity drawdowns vs consumption growth

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: his views while by no means solely responsible um contributed importantly to the lack of of you know of financial stability regulation that we ultimately paid a very heavy price for in the financial crisis.
claims.claim: Greenspan's belief that markets self-discipline contributed to weak financial-stability regulation that led to the GFC, despite excellent macro management.
claims.testable: no - historical judgement

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the financial market interventions when the market seizes up to stabilize the financial system as well as these non-standard forms of central banking QE and so on. You know these arguably saved the world twice.
claims.claim: Bernanke-era tools (market backstops when markets seize, QE, forward guidance) stopped a return to the Great Depression after the GFC and were reused for COVID.
claims.conditions: when markets seize up
claims.testable: partly - crisis episodes, few observations

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the Fed needed to keep rates uh very low for much longer than many people thought in order to try to foster a fuller labor market recovery.
claims.claim: After the GFC structural headwinds meant rates had to stay low much longer than most expected to achieve a full labor-market recovery, and doing so worked.
claims.conditions: after balance-sheet recessions with structural headwinds
claims.testable: partly - one historical episode

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: he was willing to effectively backs stop private sector borrowing, not just government bonds. And in doing so, he he prevented a financial crisis on the order of the GFC
claims.claim: In 2020 the Fed backstopped private-sector borrowing, not just Treasuries, which prevented a GFC-scale financial crisis.
claims.conditions: acute market seizure
claims.testable: yes - credit spreads around March 2020 facility announcements

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Now there will be always uh you know some mark against Jay Powell for the fact that the Fed was slow to grasp the strength and persistence of inflation after the pandemic and then had to play catchup.
claims.claim: After the pandemic the Fed was slow to recognize inflation persistence, then caught up with a very fast tightening cycle and QT.
claims.conditions: after large shocks
claims.testable: partly - one episode; reaction lag measurable

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Jay Powell achieved something that most economists thought was unreachable which was to bring inflation down without pushing unemployment up by any meaningful amount.
claims.claim: The 2022-23 tightening brought inflation down without a meaningful rise in unemployment, defying the near-universal 2022 recession consensus.
claims.testable: yes - consensus recession probability vs outcomes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: launches a trade war, which of course uh creates at least an initial wave of inflation because imported prices shoot up
claims.claim: A tariff-driven trade war creates an initial wave of inflation through higher import prices, which later rolls over.
claims.testable: yes - import price and CPI response to tariff dates

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: if you look at the markets on a daily basis, they simply move with oil prices and the yield on the 10-year.
claims.claim: In the current regime stocks move day to day with oil prices and the 10-year yield.
claims.direction: oil and yields up -> stocks down
claims.conditions: during the oil shock and rising-yield regime
claims.testable: yes - rolling daily correlations
